findings.summary: The stub hub's port knobs have no path to the candidate: the hub's address has two sources of truth
findings.recommendation: guest.conf exposes SOAK_MEDUSA_HTTP_PORT and SOAK_MEDUSA_WS_PORT, and guest-setup.sh leases them, binds the stub hub on them and health-checks it there. But the candidate finds the hub only through its own MEDUSA_BRIDGE_HTTP_URL (lib/medusa.js, default http://localhost:3009), and nothing in setup or the runbooks sets that variable or checks it against the knob. If an operator changes SOAK_MEDUSA_HTTP_PORT (which the lease refusal, 'another service may hold it', invites them to do), setup still ends 'guest ready ... stub hub on N/N+1', and then every engine.session.medusa-cycle ends NOT_LISTENING against a hub the candidate never dials. SOAK_MEDUSA_WS_PORT is also redundant: setup refuses any value other than HTTP+1, so it is a derived value presented as a setting. Scope: instance. Fix it with one source of truth. Either drop both knobs and pin the stub to the candidate's default (derive the WS port inside setup), or keep one HTTP-port knob and make setup refuse when the candidate's effective bridge URL is not http://localhost:<that port>. The README and guest.conf wording then follows from whichever you choose.

findings.summary: Stub hub port-lease refusal throws away the registry's reason and guesses one
findings.recommendation: Scope: instance. In guest-setup.sh step 6 the lease call runs curl with `-o /dev/null`, so on any status other than 200/201 setup prints `leasing port N for the stub hub answered <status>: another service may hold it`. The registry puts the cause in the body: 409 PORT_CONFLICT names the owning project and service, 409 PORT_IN_USE names the listener's pid and command (for example a hub a previous run left bound with no lease record), and a 400 names the field it rejected. That body is dropped, and for a 400 or a 5xx the added guess is wrong. On the dry run, an operator who hits this refusal goes looking for another port holder when the registry has already said what went wrong, or refused the request body. This branch already fixed the same gap for step 5 (commit 178435b8 keeps the setup reply body because 'a refusal names its cause ... only there'). Apply that to the lease loop: keep the body in a temp file, append its `code`/`error` (and `owner`/`listener` when present) to the refusal, and only say 'another service may hold it' for a 409. The existing step-6 refusal test in test/soak-guest.test.js can then check that a 409 PORT_CONFLICT fake's owner appears in the refusal.

findings.summary: The stub's roster and queues keep every workspace ever registered
findings.recommendation: Instance. In deploy/soak/medusa-stub/medusa-stub.js, `known` and `queues` are never pruned. Every medusa-cycle mints two new workspace ids, so over a 72-hour run `GET /workspaces` lists every workspace that has ever registered, including dead ones, rather than the live clients. Nothing in the soak schedule reads the roster, and the queues empty on ack, so nothing breaks today. If you want the roster to reflect live clients, answer `/workspaces` from `sockets` (keep `known` only for the 404 check). Otherwise accept.

findings.summary: The upgrade handler drops bytes that arrive with the handshake
findings.recommendation: Instance. `onUpgrade(req, socket)` ignores the upgrade event's third argument (`head`). A client that pipelines its first frame with the handshake would lose that frame. Node's WebSocket client (undici), which the candidate uses, sends nothing until it has the 101, so this has no effect today. Seed `client.buf` with `head` if the stub ever serves another client.
